title: Micah 2:1–13
context: Micah pronounces woe on those who plan evil at night and seize fields and houses by day (2:1–2). The LORD answers with his own plan of disaster, so that the land-grabbers lose their land and their place in the LORD’s assembly (2:3–5). Opponents try to silence the prophet (2:6–7), while the people prey on travelers, women, and children (2:8–10), preferring a prophet of wine and strong drink (2:11). The chapter closes with a promise of the LORD gathering the remnant of Israel like sheep, with their king and the LORD at their head (2:12–13). Most readers take 2:12–13 as a promise of restoration; some read it as the false prophets’ comforting words, continuing 2:11.

verses.text: Woe to those who devise iniquity and work evil on their beds! When the morning is light, they practice it, because it is in the power of their hand.
verses.arminianNotes: “Woe to those who devise iniquity and work evil on their beds!” Arminian readers see sin planned at night and carried out by day by those who have the power to do it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see deliberate wickedness rooted in the heart. Shared ground: the oracle condemns the misuse of power, showing that God sees not only deeds but the plans behind them.

verses.text: They covet fields and seize them, and houses, then take them away. They oppress a man and his house, even a man and his heritage.
verses.arminianNotes: “They covet fields and seize them, and houses, then take them away.” Arminian readers see the tenth commandment broken and families robbed of their heritage.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see covetousness leading to oppression. Shared ground: land in Israel was a family inheritance under the LORD (compare Leviticus 25:23), so seizing it attacked the household’s place in the covenant.

verses.text: Therefore the LORD says: “Behold, I am planning against these people a disaster, from which you will not remove your necks, neither will you walk haughtily, for it is an evil time.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “Behold, I am planning against these people a disaster.” Arminian readers see the measure-for-measure response: those who plan evil face the LORD’s plan of judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s just counterplan. Readers in this tradition note the wordplay between the oppressors’ devising in 2:1 and the LORD’s planning here.

verses.text: In that day they will take up a parable against you, and lament with a doleful lamentation, saying, ‘We are utterly ruined! My people’s possession is divided up. Indeed he takes it from me and assigns our fields to traitors!’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: “In that day they will take up a parable against you,” lamenting that their fields are divided. Arminian readers see the land-grabbers losing their own land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the reversal of fortunes. Those who took fields will see their fields taken, and readers in this tradition see God’s justice matching the punishment to the crime.

verses.text: Therefore you will have no one who divides the land by lot in the LORD’s assembly.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore you will have no one who divides the land by lot in the LORD’s assembly.” Arminian readers see the oppressors excluded from the future allotment of the land among God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see exclusion from the covenant inheritance. The allusion is to the division of the land by lot in Joshua, and readers in this tradition see the loss of a place among God’s people.

verses.text: “Don’t prophesy!”—they prophesy— “Don’t prophesy about these things. Disgrace won’t overtake us.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Don’t prophesy!”—they prophesy— “Don’t prophesy about these things.” Arminian readers see opponents of Micah trying to silence his warnings while claiming that disgrace will not overtake them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see resistance to the prophetic word. Shared ground: those who want comfortable messages often reject warnings, a pattern seen throughout the prophets.

verses.text: Shall it be said, O house of Jacob, “Is the LORD’s Spirit angry? Are these his doings? Don’t my words do good to him who walks blamelessly?”
verses.arminianNotes: “Is the LORD’s Spirit angry? Are these his doings? Don’t my words do good to him who walks blamelessly?” Arminian readers see the LORD answering that his words bless those who walk uprightly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s word as good to the upright. Readers in this tradition note that the harshness of the message reflects the people’s sin, not a defect in God’s character.

verses.text: But lately my people have risen up as an enemy. You strip the robe and clothing from those who pass by without a care, returning from battle.
verses.arminianNotes: “But lately my people have risen up as an enemy.” Arminian readers see the LORD’s people acting like enemies, robbing peaceful travelers of their clothing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the people behaving as enemies toward their own neighbors. Shared ground: injustice within God’s people is treated as hostility toward God himself.

verses.text: You drive the women of my people out from their pleasant houses; from their young children you take away my blessing forever.
verses.arminianNotes: “You drive the women of my people out from their pleasant houses.” Arminian readers see the vulnerable dispossessed and their children deprived of the LORD’s blessing.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see oppression of women and children condemned. Readers in this tradition hear in “my blessing” the LORD’s claim on the inheritance that the oppressors have stolen.

verses.text: Arise, and depart! For this is not your resting place, because of uncleanness that destroys, even with a grievous destruction.
verses.arminianNotes: “Arise, and depart! For this is not your resting place, because of uncleanness that destroys.” Arminian readers see exile announced to those who defiled the land.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the land no longer a place of rest for the unfaithful. Readers in this tradition note the irony: those who drove others out will themselves be driven out.

verses.text: If a man walking in a spirit of falsehood lies, saying, “I will prophesy to you of wine and of strong drink,” he would be the prophet of this people.
verses.arminianNotes: “If a man walking in a spirit of falsehood lies, saying, ‘I will prophesy to you of wine and of strong drink,’ he would be the prophet of this people.” Arminian readers see a people who prefer pleasant lies.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see false prophets welcomed for their comfortable messages. Shared ground: readers in both traditions commonly hear a warning against preaching that tells people what they want to hear.

verses.text: I will surely assemble all of you, Jacob. I will surely gather the remnant of Israel. I will put them together as the sheep of Bozrah, as a flock in the middle of their pasture. They will swarm with people.
verses.arminianNotes: “I will surely assemble all of you, Jacob. I will surely gather the remnant of Israel.” Arminian readers commonly read a promise of the LORD gathering his people after judgment, like sheep in a pasture.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise often read a promise of restoration. Some readers instead take 2:12–13 as the false prophets’ comforting words, continuing 2:11; readers in this tradition hold both readings as possible.

verses.text: He who breaks open the way goes up before them. They break through the gate, and go out. Their king passes on before them, with the LORD at their head.
verses.arminianNotes: “He who breaks open the way goes up before them.” and “with the LORD at their head.” Arminian readers see the LORD leading his people out, breaking through obstacles as their king.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD as king and leader of his people. Many in this tradition hear a picture fulfilled in Christ, while noting that those who read 2:12–13 as false prophecy take the verse differently.
